opening.headline: Understand the structure of gateways and common searches that enable multiple teams to connect and use models and tools from a single point of control and visibility.
body: If each team calls a different model API key in the code, the security team does not know which MCP server and tool the agent is accessing, and usage and costs are scattered across teams and cannot be combined, where should we start? As connections increase, there are more uncontrollable sideways rather than doors to control.

In this class, we will first look at the structure of Agent Gateway, which enforces policies at the entrance and exit of agent communication. We then look at the role of routing and inference gateways that divide requests to model servers based on criteria, and analyze how document permissions should be followed in a common search that ties together documents from multiple repositories.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain what a gateway does: routing, filtering, and usage aggregation.
You can analyze the structure that reflects document rights in public searches.
Distinguish between the meaning of prompt injection, mTLS, and workload identity, and explain which controls on the gateway each lead to.
Describe the place of indexes, similarity searches, and authority filters in creating search augmentations, and state why prefilters are necessary.

screens.title: Models and tools are interconnected
screens.lead: The lines in the picture are the connections between teams, models, and tools. Select the items below one by one to see with which key each connection goes out and without any supervision.

visual.alt: Complex line drawings with multiple teams and agents directly connected to models and tools without gateways.
labels: No record of who does what
I want to control my models and tools in one place

items.prompt: Line 1: Each team inserts a different model API key into the code and calls it directly.
items.answer: If each team creates their own keys and adds them to the code, there is no way to know in one place how many keys there are and who uses them. Even if one key is leaked, it is difficult to track which services are affected. Calls go straight to the model provider, so there is no point in the middle for the organization to check or block.

items.prompt: Line 2: The security team does not know which MCP servers and tools the agent is accessing.
items.answer: Agents call tools and connect to internal and external MCP servers, APIs, and other agents. Without access lists, security teams cannot see if data is going to unauthorized servers or if malicious instructions are mixed in with tool responses.

items.prompt: Line 3: Usage and costs are scattered across teams and cannot be aggregated.
items.answer: As calls go out on their own routes, usage records are also left in their respective logs. To see company totals, logs need to be collected and matched each time, and setting limits for each team becomes virtually impossible.

items.prompt: What they have in common: All three lines do not pass through a single point.
items.answer: The roots of all three problems are the same. There is no single point through which all communications pass, so there is no place to enforce policy or collect records. The gateway is the component that makes that point.

screens.outro: Now that we know what the problem looks like, let's think about a similar experience.

screens.title: Think about it: where to put a door
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: I want to control my models and tools in one place. Have you ever experienced a similar situation?
items.answer: Most organizations where multiple teams use the same model or tool experience this at least once. The first thing to check at this time is whether you can see ‘what connections exist now’ at a glance. If you can't see it, you need to make a list before controlling it.

items.prompt: Was there then a single point through which all traffic passed, or not?
items.answer: Without a single point, each team would need to manage firewall exceptions, key management, and log collection separately. Just as a reverse proxy brings together the ingress points in a general web service, the communication between models and tools also brings together the ingress and egress points so that policies and records can be handled at once.

items.prompt: Who was responsible if an in-house document search resulted in documents that you were not authorized to view?
items.answer: It's common for search systems, document owners, and rights managers to think of each other as each other's job. The second half of the lesson covers how to structure this responsibility, carrying a document's access information with an index and tracking changes to the original.

screens.outro: Now let's look at where and what Agent Gateway controls.

screens.title: Gateway security terminology: prompt injection, mTLS, workload identity
screens.lead: When you select a card, it flips over and a description appears. Use the right arrow to move to the next card and first organize the security terminology to be used in the gateway description.

cards.front: Prompt Injection: Data is read like commands
cards.back: The model reads the instructions given by the developer and the data to be processed in one text flow. So, user input or sentences in documents, web pages, or tool responses can be interpreted as instructions and change the model's behavior. This risk is classified as LLM01 on OWASP's LLM Application Risk List. So, we need a device to check what is coming and going.

Direct injection is when what the user writes in the input window changes the behavior of the model. Indirect injection is when instructions are hidden in external content read by the model, such as a web page, file, or tool response. In this case, the user's behavior changes even though he or she did not write anything malicious. Even text that is invisible to the human eye becomes effective when the model interprets it.

cards.front: TLS and mTLS: One-sided and two-sided confirmation
cards.back: In plain TLS, the client checks the server's certificate to know that the server is real and encrypts the connection. In mTLS (mutual TLS), the server also requests a certificate from the client, so both sides authenticate each other. The TLS 1.3 specification also allows servers to request client certificates and defines client authentication as optional. Between the agent and the tool, a certificate is used to verify who the caller is.

Agents are not people, but running software, or workloads. Login with human accounts is not feasible, so each workload requires a unique identity. SPIFFE is the standard for this, where the SPIFFE ID is a URI in the form spiffe://trustdomain/workloadidentifier. SVID is a document that cryptographically proves the ID and takes the form of an X.509 certificate or JWT. If each agent has an ID, you can distinguish who made the call and use it for access control and audit records.

cards.front: DPoP: Tokens cannot be used by just stealing them
cards.back: DPoP (RFC 9449) is a method of tying an OAuth access token to a key pair on the client. The client sends a certificate signed with its private key with each request, and the server verifies that the proof matches the key tied to the token. Even if the token is leaked, it cannot be used without the private key. Here, just remembering it at the terminological level is enough.

Prompt injection is a matter of instructions hidden in the content being exchanged, so content inspection takes care of it. mTLS and DPoP are devices that cryptographically verify that the person using the connection and token is correct. The SPIFFE ID is a label that indicates who the workload, called agent, is. Remember that these three answer different questions, so move on to the next screen.

screens.outro: Now that we have the terminology out of the way, let's look at Agent Gateway, which brings these devices together in one place.

screens.title: Agent Gateway: Entrance and exit for all agent communications
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare what each controls in the incoming and outgoing directions.

visual.alt: A diagram showing that both the incoming direction from the client to the agent and the outgoing direction from the agent pass through the Agent Gateway.
labels: Internal and external MCP servers, tools, API

states.label: Client-to-Agent (ingress)
states.body: The direction from which the client enters the agent or tool. When clients such as Cursor, Claude Code, or Gemini CLI connect to agents running on Google Cloud, Agent Gateway acts as a front door. It is at this point that we control which clients can access which agents and what security policies should be applied to this interaction. Developers who create agents do not need to implement access control in each agent code.

states.label: Agent-to-Anywhere (egress)
states.body: The direction in which the agent heads out. Agents running on Google Cloud enforce access permissions and security guardrails when they communicate with servers, other agents, tools, and APIs wherever they reside. At this point, you can prevent agents from sending data to unauthorized tools. The gateway handles the mTLS handshake and termination to create encrypted connections between agents and tools, and allows developers to use protocols such as MCP, A2A, REST, and gRPC of their choice.

screens.outro: Now that we have identified the entrance and exit, let's look at the control parts that make up the gateway one by one.

screens.title: Control parts that make up the gateway
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to check the parts one by one. Each part responds to one question: ‘who, where, and what?’, and all five parts must be in place for control and recording to be established together.

steps.title: Agent Identity: Who requested it
steps.body: Each agent is given a unique and secure ID (SPIFFE ID). This ID serves as the agent's digital signature for authentication, access control, and auditing. Agent identity is secured by default with context-aware access and enforces end-to-end password authentication with mTLS and DPoP.

steps.title: Agent Registry: Where are you approved to go?
steps.body: A central list of your organization's approved agents, tools, MCP servers, and endpoints. Agent Gateway checks permissions with this list before allowing the connection. This registry is the essence of centrally managing connectors.

steps.title: IAM unified access policy: what actions are allowed
steps.body: Access rules that link an agent's identity to tools and endpoints registered in the registry. If an explicit IAM policy does not allow access, all connections are blocked by default. Because it is a whitelist system, new sideways will start off as unopened. This goes hand in hand with a long-standing general principle of security design. Among the design principles outlined by Saltzer and Schroeder, fail-safe defaults are to set the default value for access judgment to 'no access if not permitted'. Added to this is the principle of least privilege (NIST SP 800-53 AC-6), which grants only as much authority as is necessary for the job. OWASP classifies giving LLM applications more functionality, power, or autonomy than necessary as a risk called Excessive Agency (LLM06). The purpose of default blocking is to ensure that even if the model is manipulated or misjudged, the damage remains within an acceptable range.

steps.title: Model Armor: What's at stake?
steps.body: This is a content security filter attached to the gateway. It inspects user prompts and tool responses in real time to prevent prompt injection, leakage of sensitive information, and harmful content. You can configure the template to block and hide policy-violating content, or you can configure it to only scan and log.

steps.title: Agent Observability: What Happened?
steps.body: The gateway creates observable data of all agent interactions at the network layer and exports them to Agent Observability. Cloud Logging and Cloud Trace enable security investigation and performance monitoring. Because controls and records come from the same point, no gaps are left behind during follow-up.

screens.outro: Next, let's look at the routing side, which determines where to send the request.

screens.title: Role of model routing and inference gateway
screens.lead: Select each tab to see how the generic proxy, agent gateway, and inference gateway divide the same request.

tabs.label: generic proxy
tabs.body: As you can see from NGINX's proxy module, the framework of a reverse proxy is simple. With `proxy_pass`, the request is passed to the back server, and with `proxy_next_upstream`, when an error or timeout occurs, the next server is tried. The default values ​​are error and timeout. This is the basic concept of routing: splitting from one inlet to a back server and diverting failures to another server. When a server is overloaded, standard HTTP signals with status codes. 429 Too Many Requests means that too many requests were sent within a certain period of time. You can add a Retry-After header to the response to indicate how soon you will try again. You can also use the same header for 503 Service Unavailable. Routing rules can use these standard signals as a guide to route the call to another server or tell the caller to wait.

tabs.label: agent gateway
tabs.body: Agent Gateway builds identity and policy on the same framework. When a request comes in, we check who sent it, determine if it can go to the registry's approval list and IAM policy, and only send it to places that are allowed. The routing of this gateway does not simply divide the load, but determines where it can be sent.

tabs.label: Inference Gateway
tabs.body: Inference gateways adapt routing concepts to model servers. Model servers have different load characteristics from regular web servers. The processing time for each request can vary greatly, so dividing the number of requests evenly can overwhelm one server. So, criteria such as model type, request size, team and purpose, and server status are declared as rules and sent to the appropriate model or server.

tabs.label: Usage Aggregation
tabs.body: Since all requests pass through the inlet, usage is pooled at the inlet. Since you can aggregate by team and model, it becomes easier to set limits for each team and add up company-wide costs. What was impossible when the keys were spread out becomes a basic feature when the entrance is brought together. For example, if a team's call volume suddenly increases, it's immediately visible in the tally at the entrance, so you can adjust limits or determine the cause before the bill arrives.

screens.outro: Now that we've seen the request side, let's see how the permissions should follow on the search side.

screens.title: How public search (RAG) works: index, similarity search, authority filter
screens.lead: Select the right arrows to follow the order in which documents are indexed, retrieved based on your questions, and passed to the model. At the end, it is revealed at which level the permission filter should be applied.

visual.alt: Flow chart where documents are converted into pieces and vectors and stored in an index, and questions are retrieved with permission filters and passed to the model.
labels: If you skip here, it’s already too late

steps.title: Index: Fragment a document and convert it into vectors
steps.body: Long documents are usually divided into paragraph-sized chunks and stored. Each piece goes through an embedding model and is converted into a vector, which is an array of numbers, and texts with similar meanings are made into vectors that are close to each other. Fragments can be saved with metadata such as the original document ID or permission group. The collection stored this way is the index.

steps.title: Search: Convert questions into vectors to find nearby pieces
steps.body: When the user asks a question, we convert the question into a vector in the same way and pick the top few (top-k) pieces that are closest to the index. Because it doesn't look at whether the keywords are the same, but whether the meaning is close, it can be found even if the expressions are different. This architecture, which combines a generative model with a device for searching dense vector indices, was summarized by Lewis et al. in a 2020 paper as retrieval augmented generation (RAG).

steps.title: Generate: Pass the found pieces to the model along with a question.
steps.body: The pieces found are attached to a prompt along with a question and are passed to the model, which summarizes or answers based on its content. There is an important property here. The model can use all received fragments as a basis, so if fragments that it does not have permission to see are mixed in, their content will be incorporated into the response sentence. Once the content has been incorporated, it is difficult to filter it out sentence by sentence later.

steps.title: Permission filters are applied before searching.
steps.body: Pre-filtering is a method of putting the user's group in the search criteria to select only the allowed fragments as candidates. Post-filtering involves picking out the top fragments first and then deleting the unauthorized ones. Assuming that 4 out of the top 5 pieces are unauthorized pieces, the post-filter leaves only 1 piece, making the answer poor, and even if there are more allowed pieces after that, they are not nominated. It is already too late to filter after the model has summarized. OWASP also recommends permission-aware vector storage and data separation by user group.

steps.title: Why are original permissions reflected late in the index?
steps.body: The index is a copy of the original repository. When access rights change in the source, the permission groups in the index must also be updated. This update is accomplished by synchronizing at certain intervals or receiving and processing change events. So, there is a gap between the time the original is changed and the time the index is changed, and in the meantime, searches are performed using the old authority. For example, if your home synchronization interval is one hour, employees who may be away for up to an hour may see old documents.

steps.title: Organizing: Filters, Access Information, Sync Interval
steps.body: You just need to remember three things. Permission filters are applied before searching, access information is loaded into the index along with fragments, and the synchronization interval between the source and index is managed with a value that determines the risk level of permission propagation. In the next screen, you will see what this principle looks like on a single document stored in the index.

screens.outro: Now that we know how search works, let's see where the permission information is for a single document stored in the index.

screens.title: Public discovery and permission propagation
screens.lead: Below is an example of a single document stored in a public search index. Select the underlined passages to see what role each field plays in protecting your rights.

visual.alt: A diagram showing that when two users enter the same query, they receive different search results depending on their access rights.

data.text:
Document ID: contract-0042  
Owned Division: Division A  
Allowed group: group-biz-a  
Original Repository: Contract Documents Repository  
Permission renewal time: Updated according to original changes  
Main text: Summary of supply agreement terms

marks.note: The index should include not only the text but also who can view it. When searching, this value should be matched against the user's group to filter results to prevent unauthorized documents from being mixed into the summary.
If you add the ownership unit to each document as metadata, it will serve as a standard when dividing the index by business division or applying filters.

marks.span: Permission renewal time: Updated according to original changes
marks.note: If permissions change in the source, the access information in the index must also change accordingly. This is permission propagation. If transmission is delayed or missed, search results become a path for information leakage to retired or relocated employees.

marks.span: Main text: Summary of supply agreement terms
marks.note: Indexing only the content and discarding the access information results in the same result for all users. The danger of public search comes not from content but from missing access information.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the structure, let’s apply it to the case of separating business units.

screens.title: Commentary 1: Structuring the request for division separation
screens.lead: This is a situation where two business units use a common knowledge base but cannot see each other's documents. Select the right arrow to follow the instructor's commentary.

steps.title: Reduce your request to two sentences
steps.body: The request is twofold. The knowledge base is shared, and business units are prevented from seeing each other's documents. Common means using the index and search functions together, and separation means dividing the documents shown in the results. The two demands are not in conflict, but you have to decide where they divide.

steps.title: Add ownership and permission information to documents
steps.body: First, check whether the owning business unit and permitted group can be added as metadata to each document. Without this information, nothing can be filtered out in later steps. If access information depends on only a few documents, you should also decide at this stage whether the non-accessed documents should be open to all or closed to all. In the same step, we also check whether the access information that the original repository already has can be moved to the index.

steps.title: Enforcing Identity at the Entrance
steps.body: Search requests must always be accompanied by the identity of the user or group. If you let apps attach their own identities, one app's mistake will ruin the whole, so it's safer to block unidentified requests at entrances such as gateways.

steps.title: Decide whether to split the index
steps.body: Compare the costs and risks of whether to divide the index by business unit or keep it as one and apply filters. Splitting lowers the risk of leakage between business units, but increases operating costs by increasing the index. If left alone, operation is simple, but a mistake in one line of the filter will soon result in a leak.

steps.title: Instructor's Conclusion
steps.body: If sensitivity is high, separate the indexes, if sensitivity is low, choose a single index and filter. Either way, you need to have a path for permission changes from the origin to propagate to the index, and you need to check the latency of this path.

screens.outro: This time, we will solve the tool-side problem of connector management in the same way.

screens.title: Commentary 2: Centrally managing connectors
screens.lead: The teams are each using their own MCP servers. Select the arrows to the right to follow the steps: Enroll, Attach Policy, and Check.

steps.title: First make a list
steps.body: Register the tools and MCP servers you are using with the Agent Registry to create a list. The problem was that we didn't know what the connection was, so the first step was identification, not control. Only registered items become approved destinations.

steps.title: Connecting identity and registry through policy
steps.body: Associate the agent's identity and registry entries with an IAM-integrated access policy. Connections that are not in the policy are blocked by default, so only the connections that need to be allowed are opened one by one. It's uncomfortable at first, but the sideways don't grow out of it. This is also a way to reduce excess privileges. Even if the agent is manipulated or misjudged, the damage can only be done to the extent of the connections it has left open.

steps.title: Allowed paths are also checked
steps.body: Even though it is an allowed route, it does not mean that the content is safe. Because responses from permitted tools can contain malicious instructions, attach a Model Armor template to the gateway to inspect prompts and tool responses. Templates can be configured to block and mask, or just scan and log, and violation records can be viewed on the Model Armor page and Security Command Center.

steps.title: Know your limits and use them
steps.body: There are limitations to this integration. Document and file uploads are not subject to inspection by this integration and must be handled as separate APIs. If you don't know this and assume your document uploads are protected, you're missing the biggest hole. Model Armor and integration services must be deployed in the same region, and inline protection in the transmission direction is limited to MCP servers, services that follow the OpenAI format, and A2A integration.

steps.title: Instructor's Conclusion
steps.body: The three layers of registration, default blocking, and content inspection maintain a level of control as the number of connectors grows. However, since one part does not block all types of input, the unsupported range must be supplemented by other means.

screens.outro: Lastly, let's read the order in which requests flow in a schematic diagram.

ext.title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications: LLM06 Excessive Agency

screens.title: Commentary 3: Reading the composition as a single page
screens.lead: If you hover over or select an underlined term in the text, you will see instances where you are stuck at that step and the remaining history.

data.text: When a request arrives at the gateway, it is first processed by Your identity is verified. Once identity is verified, the registry and access policies determine whether the identity is authorized to reach the destination via Allowed?. If authorized, it proceeds through Content Inspection and is routed to the appropriate model or tool via routing. Records from all these stages flow to an observability tool, enabling investigation into exactly which step and decision was made in the event of an incident.

terms.tip: Unidentified or forged requests stop here. What remains: Who and when the rejected request was made.
Connections to destinations not in the registry or not permitted by policy are blocked by default here. A record is left: which identity attempted which destination.
Requests and responses containing prompt injection or sensitive information are filtered out here. Remaining record: Model Armor's violation decision.
The destination is determined based on criteria such as model type, request size, team and purpose. Records remaining: which model and server went to, usage amount.

screens.outro: I will finish by organizing the structure one more time.

screens.title: Takeaway: Make things control and visible from one place
screens.lead: We will organize what we have seen so far into one standard.

paragraphs: Agent Gateway enforces policies at the ingress and egress of agent communications. It handles both the incoming and outgoing directions of the client to the agent at one point, and handles mTLS and protocol conversion for you, reducing the burden on developers.

The gateway ties together identity, registry, access policy, content inspection, and observability. Each of these five parts responds to the questions of who is there, where, what can be done, what is communicated, and what happened.

The routing and inference gateway divides requests into model servers based on criteria and aggregates usage at the ingress. The key is not speed, but control and visibility. Another important advantage of routing is that if the basis for dividing requests remains a declared rule, you can later explain why the request went to that server.

Public search must carry document access information along with an index and propagate permission changes to the original to be secure. The connector is centrally managed in the registry and left as blocked by default.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Once you have one door to control, you can handle both policies and records at once. Inside that door, identity and authority must always follow the request.

glossary.def: A component that enforces policy at the ingress and egress of communications between agents, tools, and clients.
A central list of your organization's approved agents, tools, MCP servers, and endpoints. The gateway checks this list before allowing a connection.

It is a content security filter that prevents prompt injection and leakage of sensitive information by inspecting prompts and tool responses in real time. Prompt injection is a problem in which sentences in an input or document are read as instructions to the model and change its behavior.
Rules that direct requests to the appropriate model or server based on criteria such as model type, request size, team, and purpose.
This involves reflecting changes in access rights to the original document in the access information in the search index.

mTLS is a TLS method in which the server and client authenticate each other with certificates. SPIFFE ID is a URI representation of the unique identity of a workload, such as an agent, and is used to distinguish who made the call.

misconceptions.myth: A gateway is a device that aims to increase response speed.
misconceptions.fact: The key to gateways is control and visibility. The goal is to gather all communications into one location to enforce policies and keep records.

misconceptions.myth: Once you place a document in the search index, you no longer need to worry about permissions.
misconceptions.fact: If permissions change in the source but are not propagated to the index, the document will be searchable even for users whose permissions have been lost. Access information must be carried with an index and kept up with changes.

misconceptions.myth: Accessing the tool is safe as long as you check the prompt.
misconceptions.fact: Content inspection is a device that looks at what is coming and going. Registry and access policies must separately determine which identities can access which destinations.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Agent Gateway enforces policies at the ingress and egress of agent communications.
It bundles identity, registry, access policies, content inspection, and observation, and blocks connections by default.
Routing divides requests based on criteria and pools usage in one place.
Public search is secure when it carries document access information with an index and propagates changes to the original.

checks.q: The security team tries to prevent agents from connecting to unregistered MCP servers. What is the most appropriate configuration?
options: Check tool response with only Model Armor turned on
Check the observation log daily to look for abnormal connections.
Registers approved servers in the registry and blocks connections without explicit permission by default.
Control only which agents a client accesses
checks.explain: The registry becomes an approval list, and connections that are not explicitly allowed by the access policy are blocked by default, so you can control whether or not they are allowed.

wrong.0: Model Armor is a content check and does not determine whether a connection is allowed or not.
wrong.1: Checking logs is an afterthought and cannot prevent the connection itself.
wrong.3: It only deals with the ingress from the client to the agent, and the way the agent goes out is separate.

checks.q: Which of the following is the most appropriate post-filter problem to first select the top five fragments and then delete unauthorized fragments?
options: All vectors stored in the index are changed.
Questions cannot be converted to vectors
Accepted pieces may not be nominated, resulting in poor results.
The rights of the original document are automatically revoked.
checks.explain: In the post-filter, the parent fragment is determined before the permission check, so if an unauthorized fragment takes its place, the permitted fragment is pushed out as a candidate. Therefore, a pre-filter that adds authority to search conditions is appropriate.

wrong.0: Filtering does not change the index vector itself.
wrong.1: The vector transformation in question is independent of the filter position.
wrong.3: Filters only filter results and do not change the authority of the original.

right: Central list of approved tools and MCP servers

checks.explain: Identity, listing, content inspection, and observation have different controls within a gateway.

checks.q: The key to preventing content from documents you don't have permission to see from being mixed into the public search summary?
options: Put all documents in one index and remove sensitive sentences during summarization step
Includes access information in the index and filters results based on user identity at search time
Reduce the number of search results to reduce exposure potential
Permissions are checked only once when the user first logs in.
checks.explain: Access information must be in the index and filtered by user identity at search time to ensure that unauthorized documents are not included in the summary and that changes to the original are propagated.

wrong.2: Even if the number is reduced, unauthorized documents may be included.
wrong.3: Since permissions can change from the original, they must be filtered by identity at each search time.
